articles.title: A Virginia farmer protected his land from development and persuaded his neighbours to follow; 25 years later, nearly 2,500 acres of private farms now form a wildlife corridor
articles.summary: US News: On a humid summer morning in Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley, the work of protecting nature looks surprisingly ordinary. There are fields to tend, invasi.
articles.body: On a humid summer morning in Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley, the work of protecting nature looks surprisingly ordinary. There are fields to tend, invasive plants to control and young trees to check. But across these farms, two longtime neighbors are quietly working toward something much bigger: keeping wildlife habitats connected in a landscape increasingly divided by development. According to a report by the Smithsonian Magazine, farmers John Rice and John Sessler have spent decades managing their properties not only for agriculture, but also for biodiversity. Their efforts, supported by science and conservation programs, have helped transform privately owned farmland into an important link between larger protected landscapes. The report clearly states that Rice’s conservation journey began about 25 years ago when he recognized the importance of his property’s location. His land sits along a potential connection between Massanutten Mountain and other protected areas, offering wildlife a route through an otherwise fragmented landscape. After purchasing the property, Rice placed it under a conservation easement, an agreement designed to limit future development. It became the first such easement in Page County. He then began approaching neighboring landowners and encouraging them to consider similar protections. Building trust took years, but the effort gradually expanded beyond a single property. Today, nearly 2,500 acres of privately owned land are protected in the area, creating a larger corridor where wildlife can move between habitats. Scroll down to read the details about it.Two approaches, one conservation goalRice and the Sesslers manage their farms differently, but their objectives are similar. Rice spends considerable time controlling invasive plants such as wavyleaf basketgrass and Japanese stiltgrass. These aggressive species can form dense ground cover, pushing out native plants and reducing habitat diversity. He also takes advantage of native seeds already present in his soil. By carefully managing the land, he has encouraged dormant native plant communities to return naturally.The Sesslers took a different route. When they began managing their property, they planted native seed mixes that produced fields filled with wildflowers and plants capable of supporting birds, butterflies and other pollinators. Their contrasting approaches demonstrate that there is no single formula for restoring biodiversity. Existing native vegetation can be encouraged, or new habitat can be established through intentional planting.Fighting habitat fragmentationThe need for such work is growing as development, roads, invasive species, pollution and climate change alter Virginia’s landscapes. Habitat fragmentation breaks continuous natural areas into smaller, isolated patches. For wildlife, these separated areas can function like islands, making it harder for animals to find food, reproduce and move between populations. Connected corridors can help address the problem by allowing species to travel between larger protected areas. For farms located between forests, mountains and other natural habitats, conservation agreements can therefore have an impact far beyond individual property boundaries.Using fire to restore native habitatAccording to the report, conservation work on the farms also includes prescribed burning, and controlled burns can help remove accumulated vegetation, stimulate native plant growth and maintain habitats that depend on periodic fire. Rice helped establish the Shenandoah Valley Prescribed Burn Association, giving landowners another tool for managing their properties. Used under carefully controlled conditions, prescribed fire can benefit both naturally occurring seed banks and fields planted with native species.Science helps measure the differenceThe Smithsonian’s Virginia Working Landscapes program provides another important piece of the effort, states the report. Scientists, volunteers and interns conduct biodiversity surveys on participating farms, documenting plants, birds and other species. Their findings help researchers understand how different land-management practices influence biodiversity. For landowners, the surveys also provide tangible evidence of how their work is changing the landscape. Discovering native plants and wildlife species can indicate that conservation practices are creating healthier ecosystems. The program collects information across multiple properties, allowing scientists to examine broader patterns and identify management approaches that could benefit farms throughout Virginia.A model built across property linesVirginia’s Wildlife Corridor Action Plan, introduced in 2023, recognizes the importance of reconnecting fragmented habitats and reducing threats such as wildlife-vehicle collisions. But with roughly 90% of Virginia’s land privately owned, conservation cannot depend entirely on public parks and protected areas. That makes efforts by private landowners especially significant. In the Shenandoah Valley, Rice and Sessler show how conservation can begin with individual decisions and grow through neighbors working together. Their farms remain productive, but they also provide space for native plants, pollinators, birds and other wildlife.After 25 years, what began with one farmer protecting his property has developed into a nearly 2,500-acre network of privately conserved land. It is a reminder that wildlife corridors are not always created by governments or large conservation organizations. Sometimes, they begin with a farmer looking at a map, recognizing an opportunity and convincing the people next door to join him.Images Courtesy: Smithsonian MagazineCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hurricane Katrina forced New Orleans’ Charity Hospital to close in 2005; 21 years later, the million-sq-ft building is being transformed into a $500 million medical research hub
articles.summary: US News: In 2005, when Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans, doctors at the Charity Hospital scrambled to keep patients alive without power or functioning medical.
articles.body: In 2005, when Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans, doctors at the Charity Hospital scrambled to keep patients alive without power or functioning medical equipment as floodwaters trapped them inside its darkened halls for days on end. The massive hospital that had cared for the city's residents for years was shuttered after the last patients and staff were rescued that year. Now, as Louisiana marks the storm's 21st anniversary, the long-vacant storm-damaged building is about to renew life, according to AP.A medical research hubIn summer 2026, Tulane University announced that it is spearheading a $500 million effort to convert Charity Hospital into a pioneering medical research facility, transforming the 1930s-era art deco building into a downtown hub of biomedical innovation. Construction is expected to start this fall.Tulane leaders say reviving the iconic landmark marks a major stride in putting behind the hurricane’s dark days. Charity Hospital “reflected the sort of commitment of New Orleans to the healthcare of the community,” Tulane President Michael Fitts said. “Now it’s being brought back in a way that makes the same commitment to the community.”Local leaders have embraced the project in a city where some hospitals have haunted New Orleans since Katrina. Dozens of patients died at the former Memorial hospital, now known as the Ochsner Baptist Medical Center, after floodwaters trapped them inside in sweltering conditions without power. Demolition crews this month began tearing down another complex, the Lindy Boggs Medical Center, which had sat blighted and vacant for more than 20 years after Katrina.Plans include providing space for medical and public health programs as part of what Fitts called “the largest, most significant initiative in the history of Tulane.” The new accommodations will also include labs for hundreds of researchers, space for biomedical startups, and classrooms. The new medical research hub is scheduled to be completed in 2029.Hamm said he hopes the hub will spur medical advancements that benefit the entire Gulf South. Anticipating a bright, new future for the Charity Hospital building, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno called the redevelopment “a welcome step forward and an opportunity to put this historic property back to productive use.”Past attemptsFor generations, the Charity Hospital system served as New Orleans’ safety net, treating all patients regardless of whether they had health insurance. The million-square-foot (93,000-square-meter) main building has remained empty since Katrina. Dr. Lee Hamm, dean of the Tulane University School of Medicine, recalled canoeing through the submerged city to check on the welfare of patients and health care staff. “Everyone was exhibiting a lot of courage at the moment,” Hamm said. “People were going about doing what they needed to do.”In the past decades, various redevelopment gambits have failed. The hospital was run by Louisiana State University, which determined that Katrina left the building too damaged to reopen, an assessment that was disputed by some hospital staff and community members. Instead, LSU used federal disaster relief funding to open a new hospital.One of the deadliest and most destructive hurricanes in U.S. history, Katrina killed nearly 1,400 people across five states and racked up an estimated $200 billion in damage, flattening homes along the nearby Gulf Coast and swamping entire neighbourhoods with ruinous floods.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Food regulator FSSAI on Saturday said it has prohibited Everest Food Products Pvt Ltd and Laljee Godhoo and Company from selling hing powde.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Food regulator FSSAI on Saturday said it has prohibited Everest Food Products Pvt Ltd and Laljee Godhoo and Company from selling hing powder after finding the products to be sub-standard.In a social media post, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said it had issued prohibition orders against Everest Food Products and Laljee Godhoo and Company after their hing powder products were found to be sub-standard.In the case of Everest, FSSAI has prohibited the sale of variants of compounded asafoetida (hing powder) with immediate effect."The samples of Compounded Asafoetida (Hing Powder) were found to be 'Misbranded and Sub-standard' by the Food Analyst of the primary food laboratory," the regulator said.The products were found to be in contravention of the provisions of the FSS (Food Products and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, as the alcohol-soluble extract was 0 per cent against the prescribed standard of not less than 5 per cent."The samples of Yellow Hing Powder (Compounded Asafoetida) and Black Hing Powder (Compounded Asafoetida) were also found to be Sub-standard, with Alcoholic Extract reported at 3.29 per cent and 4.4 per cent, respectively," it added, as quoted by PTI.The regulator has asked the company to submit an action plan to rectify the continued malpractice of selling substandard compounded hing/asafoetida and ensure the sale of standard products as licensed under the FSS Act, 2006.It warned of further action if the company does not rectify the mistakes.In the case of Laljee Godhoo, FSSAI said the company had been prohibited from selling hing powder after it was found to be sub-standard and adulterated, in contravention of FSSAI regulations."The samples of Compounded Hing / Compounded Asafoetida (Powder and Lump) were found to be sub-standard and not conforming to the prescribed requirements under the FSS (Food Products and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011. The compounded Hing samples were also found to be misbranded and Sub-standard," it added.The samples of raw hing varieties used in the manufacture of compounded hing were found to be sub-standard due to the presence of excess starch.The starch content in hing shall not exceed 1 per cent by weight.FSSAI has asked Laljee Godhoo to submit an action plan to rectify the malpractice and outline measures to ensure that only standard products are manufactured and sold in accordance with the FSS Act.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: New plan to end employment authorization for some spouses of H-1B visa holders:  '600,000+ jobs will open up in next 2-4 weeks'
articles.summary: US News: The Department of Homeland Security has come up with a proposal to remove certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B visa holders from employment authoriza.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security has come up with a proposal to remove certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B visa holders from employment authorization. Not much is known about the proposal and the proposal is listed as a long-term action and not to be published immediately. But it created a major confusion among H-1B visa holders while America First activists celebrated and claimed that if this gets published Monday, over 600,000 jobs will open up in next 2-4 weeks."DHS is proposing to remove from its regulations certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B nonimmigrant workers as a class of aliens eligible to request employment authorization under the (c)(26) category. This proposal would reverse the changes made in the 2015 final rule, 'Employment Authorization for Certain H-4 Dependent Spouses,' and restore DHS's long-standing policy of not extending eligibility to request employment authorization to H-4 dependent spouses," the DHS statement read.Who are H-4 visa holders?H-4 visa holders are spouses of H-1Bs in the US. They are authorized to work in the US, and they get an Employment Authorization Document based on a 2015 rule. The proposal plans to remove some H-4 visa holders from the category. It's not known who will be affected if the proposal becomes a rule, but experts believe that those who have been living in the US for a long time, waiting for Green Card may be targeted by the new rule.Are H-1B spouses banned from doing jobs in the US?As this is only a proposal and will take months and years to become approved, H-1B spouses or H-4 visa holders are not banned from jobs in the US.What should H-4 visa holders do now? Immigration experts says 'don't panic'Immigration expert Swatilina Barik said there is no need to panic today, based on the agenda entry, as it is only a statement of intent and not a rule. "Before anything changes, DHS must publish a proposed rule, collect public comments, respond to them, publish a final rule, and set an effective date. That takes many months at minimum, and rules like this are usually challenged in court," Barik said."What is true today: Your work permit is still valid. USCIS is still accepting and deciding I765 applications under current rules. Nothing changed for you this week.""What you can do: Renew early. Automatic extensions ended for several categories in late 2025, so filing on time no longer protects you from a gap. Know your other options before you need them. H1B, O1, national interest waiver, or a permit tied to a pending green card. One conversation with an attorney now saves you a scramble later.""Keep your documents in one place. Priority date, I140 notice, passport, status paperwork," Barik said."Employers, find out how many people on your team rely on this permit. When a proposed rule comes out, employer comments carry real weight," she suggested to employers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: On the morning of August 26, high in Langtang National Park near Nepal’s border with China, a massive wall of ice and rock suddenly broke loose.Within minutes, it had transformed into a violent debris flow and flood surge, racing almost 100 km down the Lende Khola, Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. It tore through villages on both sides of the frontier, obliterated the Rasuwagadhi border complex and left a trail of destruction in its wake.There was no earthquake.The US Geological Survey initially recorded a magnitude 4.4 tremor, only to retract it. The apparent “earthquake” had not shaken the mountain — the collapsing mass itself had generated the seismic signal. The event was later upgraded to magnitude 5.2.There was no rainfall trigger either; and, crucially, there was almost no warning.Speed defined the disaster. Readings relayed by the World Meteorological Organisation show that the Trishuli River at Galchhi rose by as much as nine metres in just 30 minutes; at Malekhu, it rose seven metres over a similar period.By the morning of August 29, Nepal’s disaster authority, NDRRMA, had put the toll at 626 dead and 2,426 missing, with more than 3,700 rescued.China separately reported seven dead and 554 missing across the border in Tibet.The destruction stretched far beyond the immediate flood zone. Twelve hydropower plants were reportedly knocked offline, dozens of bridges were swept away and the only road connecting the valley to the rest of Nepal was destroyed.But the Rasuwa disaster was not an isolated event. It was the latest and deadliest expression of a question Nepal has repeatedly had to confront:Why does a country so accustomed to natural disasters remain so vulnerable when they strike?Not the firstThe Rasuwa flood sits inside a documented, decades-long pattern.Nepal’s disaster authority recorded more than 32,000 separate incidents between 2018 and 2024 alone, killing almost 3,700 people across a wide range of hazards, including earthquakes, floods, landslides, avalanches and glacial outbursts.The defining event remains the 2015 Gorkha earthquake. The magnitude 7.8 quake killed 8,896 people and caused roughly $7 billion in damage, equivalent to nearly a third of Nepal’s economy at the time. It also triggered a rockfall-avalanche and air blast that levelled the village of Langtang, killing more than 350 people.Other disasters illustrate the range of threats.The 2014 Jure landslide dammed the Sunkoshi River and killed 156 people. The 1985 Dig Tsho glacial lake outburst flood destroyed a nearly completed hydropower plant. In 2021, rainfall and two landslides sent roughly 13 million cubic metres of debris downstream in the Melamchi disaster. The 2023 Jajarkot earthquake killed 154 people. And, tellingly, the same Rasuwa valley was hit by a flood in July 2025 after the sudden drainage of a glacial lake that had formed only months earlier.Against this backdrop, Germanwatch’s Climate Risk Index 2026 ranked Nepal the sixth most affected country in the world for 2024. But that finding has often been misrepresented. The index is retrospective: it measures recorded deaths, people affected and economic losses from extreme weather in a particular year, rather than vulnerability or future risk.Nepal’s 2024 ranking was driven mainly by monsoon floods and landslides across 44 districts in September, which killed 249 people and caused an estimated 46.7 billion rupees in damage. It is evidence of the scale of Nepal’s exposure to extreme weather, but it does not, by itself, explain why disasters keep occurring.The ‘underlying’ problemThe explanation begins with plate tectonics.Nepal sits directly above the boundary where the Indian plate is being driven beneath Eurasia. The collision is located along the Main Himalayan Thrust, a major fault that continues to accumulate strain and periodically releases it through large earthquakes.The Himalayas are geologically young because this collision, which began roughly 50 million years ago, is still pushing the range upwards. Unlike older, heavily eroded mountain belts, the Himalayas have had relatively little time to soften. The result is some of the steepest terrain on Earth compressed into a relatively short horizontal distance.That combination of steep slopes and active tectonics has serious consequences. A peer-reviewed analysis of the 2015 Gorkha earthquake found that it triggered at least 25,000 landslides, closely mirroring the extent of the fault rupture. The worst damage occurred where three factors overlapped: steep slopes, heavy rainfall and proximity to the deepest rupture.Crucially, more than half of the landslide debris came to rest in stream channels, leaving rivers seeded with loose material that can continue to contribute to blockages and floods years later. The steep terrain also amplifies ground shaking, meaning an earthquake of the same magnitude can cause greater damage on a high, steep slope than on flatter terrain.This helps explain why a single event in the Himalayas can rapidly become a chain of hazards. At Langtang, anomalous heavy snowfall during the preceding winter combined with minor earthquakes throughout the year may have eventually led to the rockfall-avalanche.A study of the 2021 Melamchi disaster similarly found that multiple climatic and human factors acted together at different points along the river rather than a single trigger causing the disaster.The cliché that “nature” alone is responsible therefore misses the point. The young Himalayas provide the steep terrain and seismic energy; rainfall, ice, unstable slopes and rivers determine how that energy is converted into landslides, river blockages and floods.Climate change and human activity are amplifying risksGeology provides the foundation, but a warming high-mountain environment is adding another layer of risk.Regional assessments describe changes in the Hindu Kush Himalaya cryosphere as “unprecedented and largely irreversible”. Glaciers retreated 65 per cent faster in the 2010s than in the preceding decade, while high elevations have warmed considerably faster than the global average.Warming, combined with permafrost thaw, can destabilise high-altitude rock slopes. Scientists say this can contribute to the kind of rock-ice avalanche suspected at Rasuwa. As Jakob Steiner of the University of Graz put it, “The chances that material starts to move down from mountains increase.”Scientists have nevertheless cautioned against drawing a direct line between climate change and the Rasuwa event before its precise cause is established.The picture is less straightforward when it comes to glacial lake outburst floods.The strongest available study on such floods in the Himalayas found no clear increase in their frequency in recent decades, even though scientists project that the underlying risk could roughly triple with continued glacier retreat. In other words, observed frequency and projected future risk are not necessarily moving in tandem.Rainfall trends are similarly complicated.National rainfall records from 1971 to 2015 show that extreme precipitation has, on average, weakened, even as year-to-year variability has increased.Human development, however, has clearly increased exposure.A 2018 study found that rainfall-triggered landslides were more than twice as likely within 100 metres of a road than at randomly selected locations, largely because informal road construction can oversteepen slopes and disrupt drainage.Kathmandu Valley has expanded by 4 to 6 per cent a year amid what the World Bank has described as “haphazard and unplanned urbanisation”.Governments have also repeatedly rebuilt hydropower plants, roads and border infrastructure in the same hazard-prone valleys where disasters have struck before.One popular explanation, however, does not stand up well to the evidence: deforestation. Nepal’s forest cover nearly doubled between 1992 and 2016.Nepal cannot change its geology, climate change and development, however, can alter the conditions in which hazards occur; and, crucially, determine how many people and how much infrastructure are in their path.Why hazards become disastersNepal has significantly strengthened its disaster-management architecture since 2015. It passed the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act in 2017 and created the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, or NDRRMA, in 2019.Yet there remains a gap between having institutions on paper and having systems capable of anticipating fast-moving mountain hazards. The World Bank’s 2024 assessment found Nepal’s legislative framework to be advanced, while describing its institutional arrangements for coordinating preparedness as still relatively basic.Nepal’s flood-warning systems can work effectively when monitoring the hazards they were designed to detect. Its best-performing system, on the Karnali River, can provide downstream communities with two to three hours of warning once water crosses a threshold gauge.Rasuwa presented a fundamentally different challenge.The surge crossed into Nepal at roughly 8.40am. The Flood Forecasting Division received word at 8.56am and issued a warning within four minutes. But by then, the flood had already reached much of the district. The gauging stations that were supposed to track the surge were themselves destroyed before they could transmit further information.As Shushil Kumar Shrestha, a senior NDRRMA engineer, told the New York Times: “The flood developed so rapidly that people simply did not have enough time to get to safety, even though the system was functioning.”The same preparedness gap is visible in construction. Nepal’s updated seismic code, introduced after the 2015 earthquake, still had an 89 per cent non-compliance rate recorded in 2016.The underlying gap, as experts have put it, is that Nepal is far better at tracking floods once they enter monitored rivers than at detecting the high-mountain hazards, glacier collapses, ice avalanches, landslide-dammed lakes that create them.Nepal cannot stop the Indian plate from colliding with Eurasia. It cannot prevent every unstable slope from failing thousands of metres above a remote valley.But it can narrow the gap between hazard and disaster.That means better monitoring of high-altitude slopes and glaciers, stronger early-warning networks, more resilient infrastructure, stricter construction standards, better land-use planning and evacuation systems designed for events that can unfold in minutes rather than hours.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Israeli attacks across Gaza kill two people, hit hospital supply warehouse
articles.summary: Gaza’s Health Ministry reports rising casualties amid escalated Israeli attacks, with victims trapped under rubble.
articles.body:
Several people have been wounded in an Israeli strike on a medical warehouse inside a hospital compound in central Gaza, while separate attacks killed two people elsewhere in the Strip.

The Israeli drone strike targeted a tent used as a medical supply warehouse inside the Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital complex in Deir el-Balah on Saturday, injuring three people, the hospital's director said.

The Israeli military confirmed it hit a target within the compound of Al-Aqsa Hospital, claiming without evidence that a Hamas commander was struck.

Separately, another Israeli drone struck a bike in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood. The Palestinian Wafa news agency reported that at least one person was killed and two injured in that attack. The casualties were taken to al-Quds Field Hospital.

In a separate attack earlier in the day, one person was killed by Israeli gunfire in the village of al-Musaddar, east of Deir el-Balah.

An Israeli quadcopter also dropped an explosive device in the vicinity of Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza, according to hospital officials.

Israel has escalated its attacks across the Gaza Strip in recent days despite the so-called "ceasefire".

Gaza's Health Ministry reported receiving a total of 10 bodies over the past 48 hours – nine newly killed and one recovered from under rubble – along with 18 wounded.

It said other victims remain trapped beneath destroyed buildings or on roads that ambulance and civil defence crews have been unable to reach.

Since the "ceasefire" between Israel and Hamas took effect in October last year, the ministry said, 1,313 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli attacks.

Meanwhile, between 4,000 and 5,000 Palestinians remain missing and are believed to be under rubble in Gaza, the Palestinian Centre for Missing and Forcibly Disappeared Persons said on Saturday.

It added that between 2,500 and 3,000 people may have been subjected to forced disappearance in Gaza during Israel's genocidal war.

The centre's estimate is based on an analytical study of a sample of 317 cases, and it said the findings showed indicators warranting an investigation into the possibility of a broader pattern of enforced disappearances.

Of the 317 cases examined, 302, or 95.27 percent, were male and 15 were female. The sample included 41 children and 17 people aged 60 or older.

Since Israel's war began in October 2023, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and more than 174,000 injured, most of them women and children.

articles.title: Taliban sends team to Germany to assist Afghan deportations
articles.summary: Afghanistan's Taliban authorities have temporarily sent more personnel to Germany under an agreement with the government in Berlin aimed at facilitating the...
articles.body:
Afghanistan's Taliban authorities have temporarily sent more personnel to Germany under an agreement with the government in Berlin aimed at facilitating the planned deportation of hundreds of Afghans to their home country.

"In order to achieve the objective agreed in the coalition agreement of carrying out repatriations to Afghanistan, documents must be issued that are recognized by the de facto government," the Foreign Office in Berlin stated on Saturday.

To this end, in addition to sufficient staff, the technical requirements must also be in place, particularly if the number of repatriations is to increase, the office said.

"To establish these technical requirements swiftly, a technical support team has entered the country on a short-term basis."

According to the German Interior Ministry, a total of 228 men - mainly offenders - have been deported to Afghanistan since the start of the current legislative period in March last year.

The latest group deportation by plane, carrying 23 people required to leave the country, took off from Leipzig Airport on Tuesday bound for Kabul.

To facilitate the process, the German government had authorized the temporary posting of individual Taliban-appointed diplomats to Afghanistan's diplomatic missions in Germany.

Previously, the missions had been staffed only by diplomats appointed under Afghanistan's former government.

In early June, a planned mass deportation was cancelled because the Taliban authorities refused to cooperate. They had expressed dissatisfaction with what they saw as a lack of willingness by Foreign Office representatives to engage in dialogue.

Critics, including some from the Green Party, have repeatedly reproached the German government for making concessions to facilitate deportations, despite not recognizing the Taliban government, partly because of its human rights violations, especially those affecting women and girls.

articles.title: Russian strike blows up arms depot near Kyiv, killing 37
articles.summary: Russia struck an arms depot near Kyiv overnight, sparking fires and explosions that killed 37 people and wounded dozens of others, authorities said Saturday....
articles.body:
Russia struck an arms depot near Kyiv overnight, sparking fires and explosions that killed 37 people and wounded dozens of others, authorities said Saturday.

AFP reporters saw plumes of black smoke pouring over the capital's western suburbs, while videos published by Ukraine's rescue services showed homes near the blast epicentre in flames.

The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in less than two months, with officials expressing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.

Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, pushing civilian casualties to their highest level since Moscow invaded in 2022.

"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions... ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X.

The blast forced hundreds to evacuate and damaged multiple homes, including a care facility for elderly and disabled people, he added.

At least 37 people were killed, among them the mayor of the nearby town of Dmytrivka, Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.

Residents in the area told AFP the explosion was "terrifying".

"We thought we were being bombed. No one knew it was a detonation," said Yana Doneli, resident of a nearby town.

The depot was owned by the Ukrainian military and stored drones, shells and other munitions, Zelensky said in a video address.

Zelensky blamed the incident on "horrific negligence", saying ammunition should not have been stored there.

Ukrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into criminal negligence.

"On 28 August at around 8:10 pm (1710 GMT), an unmanned aerial vehicle... fell on or struck the grounds of an enterprise in the town of Myla," the office of Ukraine's prosecutor general said.

Myla is a small town on the outskirts of western Kyiv.

"A large-scale fire broke out on the enterprise's grounds, and detonation began," prosecutors added.

The prosecutor's office said that its investigation would focus on "the legality of the... storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise's grounds", as well as whether the owner, whom it did not name, had the "necessary permits and approvals".

Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned following a previous deadly strike on a munitions depot near Kyiv in July.

That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations regarding the proximity of residential buildings.

"In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence," he said on Telegram.

"Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again."

Russia launched at least two missiles and 267 drones at Ukraine between late Friday and early Saturday, according to the Ukrainian air force.

In addition to the depot strike, Russian attacks on Ukraine killed three people on Saturday, including a two-year-old infant in Kyiv and a 14-year-old girl in the capital's outer suburbs, officials said.

In Russia, Ukrainian strikes killed three people in the Belgorod region and caused a fire at a warehouse belonging to Russian retailer Ozon, officials said.

A strike on the city of Sevastopol in Crimea killed one person, according to Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor.

US-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, Europe's deadliest since World War II, have been at a standstill for months.

Russia has demanded sweeping territorial and political concessions from Ukraine, which Kyiv has ruled out as tantamount to capitulation.

Earlier this week, US Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on an unannounced trip, amid escalating tensions in the four-and-a-half-year war.
authors: Sergei SUPINSKY, with Vadym TOMASHEVSKY in Myla

articles.title: Karnataka HC slams cops for 'illegal arrest' of activist over social media post on Kunal Kamra's show cancellation
articles.summary: BENGALURU: The Karnataka high court has pulled up Whitefield Police over the alleged illegal arrest of an activist in connection with a Facebook post .
articles.body: BENGALURU: The Karnataka high court has pulled up Whitefield Police over the alleged illegal arrest of an activist in connection with a Facebook post celebrating the cancellation of comedian Kunal Kamra’s show in Bengaluru.Justice M Nagaprasanna was hearing a petition in Mohan Gowda vs State of Karnataka and another on August 28, when the court expressed concern over the manner in which the police handled the case.During the hearing, the judge observed that "Whitefield Police Station appears to have been violating the law time and again."The case relates to a representation submitted to Whitefield Police Station by an organisation called Hindu Rashtra Samanvaya Samithi. The organisation had approached the police over Kunal Kamra’s proposed comedy show at Uru in Whitefield. The show was subsequently cancelled.Following the cancellation, the petitioner posted on Facebook that the show had been called off and described it as a "victory for Hindu unity." Police later registered a case based on the post.The petitioner’s lawyer told the court that the case was not based on a complaint from any individual but was registered 'not on a complaint by anybody but on a suo motu case registered by the Whitefield Police Station'.The court questioned the basis on which the police treated the Facebook post as a potential threat to communal harmony.It observed, "The police constable of the Whitefield Police Station gets concerned about the imaginary disharmony overnight and alleges such disharmony to be because of the post of the petitioner calling it a victory for Hindu unity."According to the proceedings, the petitioner was in Udupi at around 2 am when a police constable from Whitefield Police Station allegedly travelled there and took him into custody. He was then brought back to Whitefield Police Station and made to remain there in connection with offences under Sections 273 and 353 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).The court also questioned the manner in which the police served a notice under Section 35(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). The notice was handed to the petitioner only after he had been secured and taken into custody, at a location a short distance from Whitefield Police Station.The court noted another issue with the timing of the notice. Notices issued under Section 35(3) of the BNSS on August 5 and August 6 directed the petitioner to appear before the police within the following three days. However, by that time, he had already been taken into custody.Justice Nagaprasanna observed, "A notice indicating the later date of appearance appears to have been used to take the petitioner into custody 3 days prior to the fixed date itself. This has been the modus operandi of the policeman who mans the Whitefield Police Station,"The high court has now sought an explanation from the concerned Deputy Commissioner of Police and Assistant Commissioner of Police regarding the alleged repeated violations by the Whitefield Police.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: In 2024, England turned old fishing nets into a 16-metre footbridge; the 3.5-tonne structure needs smaller foundations and less maintenance than a conventional bridge
articles.summary: UK News: Old fishing nets seldom find a second life. But in Kent, England, the nets are being turned into something much more ambitious. The used nets have bee.
articles.body: Old fishing nets seldom find a second life. But in Kent, England, the nets are being turned into something much more ambitious. The used nets have been transformed to make a 16-metre-long footbridge to carry people over a marina entrance with minimal environmental impact during construction. Media reports from 2024 say that the Environment Agency built an innovative bridge at Twyford Marina in Yalding using recycled materials, lightweight engineering, and a construction method to reduce the amount of concrete used. The 16-metre bridge is part of the Medway Valley Walk and offers pedestrians a new route across the entrance to Twyford Marina. It also makes it easier for boats to enter and leave the marina. The bridge deck and main structure are made of fibre-reinforced polymer, or FRP, from recycled old fishing nets. The material is a blend of strength and light weight and is particularly useful in a challenging construction location. According to reports, the completed bridge is much lighter at 3.5 tons than many traditional structures of a similar size. The weight reduction also allowed engineers to use smaller support foundations.Lego-like construction systemThe innovation is not only the bridge itself. If we go by the GOV UK website, the project used modular blocks, which mostly can be placed by hand, instead of traditional reinforced-concrete retaining walls. The blocks fit together like a Lego system, with little or no mortar needed. According to experts, this method requires less reinforced concrete, making construction simpler and potentially reducing the project's carbon footprint. Lighter materials and smaller footings also allowed the bridge to be constructed in a site where it would have been difficult to deliver large construction equipment.A journey by land and seaThe bridge's journey to Kent was no less strange. According to the GOV UK website, the deck was built in the Netherlands before being shipped to Nottinghamshire and fitted with handrails. From there, the 3.5-ton structure was transported by road to Yalding. Her last voyage was by barge up the River Medway. When the bridge reached the marina, a crane set it in place. The bridge is now open to the public.Lower carbon footprint, less maintenanceAccording to the 2024 report, the Environment Agency anticipates that the recycled FRP structure will require less maintenance than a conventional bridge built from traditional materials. It’s also lighter, which means the foundations it needs are smaller. Less construction material is required, and fewer emissions are generated. In the current scenario, the project shows how infrastructure is a place where pragmatic engineering and the circular economy meet. The project has given a new lease of life to discarded fishing nets, giving them a useful second life in a structure designed to serve walkers and boat users for years. On an ordinary journey, you now pass through an extraordinary piece of environmental engineering at Twyford Marina, made from waste that once belonged to the sea.Images Courtesy: GOV UK and istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why Australia's giant cuttlefish mating season has gone silent
articles.summary: According to official figures only 1,811 cuttlefish turned up to mate this year, down 97% on last year.
articles.body:
Every winter, a sliver of the South Australian coast hosts the world's largest mating event for giant cuttlefish.

Some years, hundreds of thousands of the unique marine species endemic to Australia gather along the Cuttlefish Coast for the annual mating season, bringing their colourful, shape-shifting figures to the shallow waters and attracting thousands of keen divers.

But this year, the turnout was the lowest on record, sparking concerns of a "catastrophic decline" of the species.

Official figures released this month estimate just 1,811 cuttlefish turned up to mate this year, down from 63,000 last year - a 97% drop.

The state government says a toxic algal bloom that has ravaged the state's coastline for more than 18 months may be to blame for the sharp decline.

The low figures have also prompted calls for the species to be listed as endangered.

Adult cuttlefish typically die after breeding so each mating season is crucial for the species' future, but in recent months, just 440 eggs have been counted, instead of the millions that are usually laid.

Manny Katz, 28, was one of four divers who spent hours along the coast last month to observe the annual breeding event, having been tasked by South Australia's Department of Environment and Water (DEW).

"Because there have been so few cuttlefish, DEW thought it would be worth going out and trying to do an assessment of how many eggs there currently are around the coastline to understand what the population is going to be next year."

Over two days in July, his team did eight one-hour dives, exploring the undersides of rocky reefs to count the eggs.

"Along the eight kilometres (five miles) of coastline, there would normally be millions of eggs," he said, as each female can lay dozens of egg and tens of thousands usually turn up to breed.

"[We] pretty much looked under every single rock that we could have and we only found about 440 eggs."

Crucially, adult cuttlefish only live about 12 to 18 months, Katz said, "so the success of one breeding season is going to determine the population next year".

"Under our current circumstances, with there being so few eggs along the coastline, we don't know if the population is ever going to be able to recover."

While it's too early to tell what this means for the species' future, Katz said: "we will know that answer probably in the next year or two, whether or not this year has been a catastrophic decline."

His team also tracked adult cuttlefish numbers during the dive survey, and said the dozen or so they saw - when there should have been tens of thousands - appeared to be behaving differently.

"This year, they were all really skittish... hiding under rocks. Because there's so few cuttlefish hanging out at the moment, they don't have strength in numbers."

Katz said he wasn't shocked by the low numbers this winter given the devastating impact of the toxic algal bloom in South Australia since it was first detected in March last year.

The algal bloom - a rapid increase in the population of algae in water systems – is naturally occurring but is caused by ocean warming, marine heatwaves, and nutrient pollution - all exacerbated by climate change.

"Our marine habitats have been getting wiped out for the past year and a half now... this is an indicator that our marine ecosystems are in real big trouble - the canary in the coal mine, so to speak."

Last year's cuttlefish mating season was not impacted as the effects of the algal bloom had not yet reached the Cuttlefish Coast, Katz said, but since late last year, small concentrations of the toxic algae have been detected in the area.

This was particularly worrying as cuttlefish, along with other cephalopods like octopus and squid, are particularly vulnerable to the toxic algae.

Stefan Andrews, co-founder of the Great Southern Reef Foundation, is seeking to have the giant Australian cuttlefish listed as a threatened species given its "catastrophic decline" due to the algal bloom and the impact on the next generation.

"The harmful algal blooma is a leading plausible explanation and appears likely to have contributed, but the vailable evidence does not yet allow us to say definitively that it caused the entire decline," he said.

He said with so few adults and so little breeding activity observed, the number of young entering the population is likely to be very low.

"That will make the next breeding season especially challenging."

A spokesperson for South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said cuttlefish populations "naturally fluctuate" depending on environmental conditions.

Previous surveys have reported record lows of 13,500 in 2013 to highs of 247,000 in 2020.

"The cuttlefish population estimate rebounded to more than 100,000 just two years following the low numbers in 2013," the spokesperson said.

"While it appears likely the algal bloom has impacted cuttlefish numbers, researchers are working to determine whether this contributed to the reduced population or was just one of the potential impacts."

Prof Mike Steer, executive director of the South Australian Research and Development Institute which helped carry out the underwater surveys, said the unprecedented low estimate this year was "disheartening".

But he remained hopeful as "we know from the past that this population has the capacity to recover when conditions are favourable".

He said there were "positive signs" as adult cuttlefish were continuing to lay eggs and the population may recover "over coming years".

articles.title: Man dies in Burscough after train hits van on crossing
articles.summary: British Transport Police said a man who was in a van died at the scene, in Burscough.
articles.body:
A man has died after a train hit a van on a railway line.

The incident happened on a crossing in Burscough, West Lancashire, just after 15:00 BST.

British Transport Police (BTP) said a man who was in the van died at the scene, and two passengers on the Wigan Wallgate-Southport train suffered minor injuries.

A BTP spokesman said: "Enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

A large emergency services operation was launched, with police, fire and ambulance vehicles on the scene and in nearby farmland.

Passengers could be seen being helped down from the train by emergency services teams.

Operator Northern said there would be "major disruption", with "all lines blocked" by an "incident between Wigan Wallgate and Southport".

articles.title: Indian Standard Time to become mandatory for all entities from March 2027
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: From March next year, all entities in India will be required to use Indian Standard Time (IST) for legal, commercial, digital and administr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: From March next year, all entities in India will be required to use Indian Standard Time (IST) for legal, commercial, digital and administrative activities, with govt on Saturday notifying the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026.The rules, notified under the Legal Metrology Act, will come into force 180 days after their publication in Gazette, making IST mandatory from around March 2027. Violations of the rules will attract penalties under the Act.The notification makes IST the mandatory time reference for all legal, administrative and official documents unless specifically exempted. It also makes IST the standard time reference across commerce, transport, public administration, legal contracts and financial operations.Entities will not be allowed to use, display or record any time reference other than IST for official purposes, except where foreign time zones are clearly labelled or where alternative time sources are permitted for scientific research, navigation or astronomy.The rules are significant as modern digital infrastructure depends on microsecond-level timing accuracy. Payment systems, stock exchanges, telecom networks, 5G services, digital navigation, power grids and data centres require synchronised clocks to authenticate transactions, coordinate operations and maintain network reliability.The notification establishes a nationwide system for time synchronisation, traceability and cybersecurity, recognising accurate time as critical digital infrastructure. Under the rules, CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (NPL) will continue to maintain India’s primary time scale, UTC(NPLI), from which IST is derived, while Regional Reference Standards Laboratories (RRSLs), ISRO’s NavIC and other authorised timing sources will disseminate official time.Another major feature of the rules is the focus on cyber resilience. Organisations must deploy proper time-synchronisation systems, protect networks against spoofing, jamming and cyberattacks, integrate multiple authorised timing sources and maintain contingency mechanisms, including atomic clocks where necessary, to ensure uninterrupted operations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Norway's Haakon remembers 'my dear father' in first speech as king
articles.summary: Haakon VIII pays emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, before outlining how he wishes to reign.
articles.body:
King Haakon VIII of Norway has paid warm tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first speech to the nation since taking the throne.

"Thank you for being such a good dad," he said in an at-times emotional televised address, seated at a desk in Norway's royal palace, beside a picture of the late king, two lit candles and a bowl of white roses.

Harald, 89, who was seen as a moderniser and "people's king" during his 35-year reign, died in hospital on Friday morning after being treated for a rare blood condition.

"Now it is my turn," his 53-year-old son said, adding that a "major task" awaited him and that he wished to be "present and attentive" going forward.

Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne

Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises

Oslo mayor calls off wedding ceremony after death of Norway's king

Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".

He said Harald had been a good father to himself and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as a "warm and funny grandfather" to his six grandchildren and a "loving and caring husband" to his widow, Queen Sonja.

The new king appeared to choke back tears as he noted that Saturday would have been their 58th wedding anniversary.

Harald brought the family together "with a natural authority", of which he might not have been aware himself, his son recalled.

He had "always stayed true" to his "values and commitments", the new king stressed.

"He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own style. Be ourselves," Haakon said.

He also remarked on the "powerful and moving experience" of seeing thousands of Norwegians gather outside the royal palace in the capital Oslo with "flowers, tributes and candles".

"We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us," he said.

Norwegians have been laying flowers outside the royal palace in Oslo since news broke that Harald had died on Friday. A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet given for his funeral.

Among them was Norway's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service with his wife, Queen Mette-Marit - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer holds.

He assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.

Mette-Marit came under scrutiny when it was revealed that she had had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.

She later received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.

Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.

Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when Haakon married his mother.

Haakon's sister, Märtha Louise, has also courted controversy for remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024, their business activities ultimately leading her to step back from royal duties.

Without directly referencing these controversies, Haakon said during his speech: "Our family has experienced the importance of standing together in order to remain steadfast both within ourselves and for one another even during difficult times."

He said he, along with Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would "always strive to understand the life situations of different people".

He added: "No one who lives in this country knows what we will face together, but what we do know is that we will stand by one another through both good days and difficult ones."

Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year suggested that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

articles.title: In 1994, Hollywood Video’s founder bought 32 Oregon acres for $1.25 million and began a 52,000-sq-ft mansion; nearly 30 years and 3 owners later, it is still unfinished and asking $4.7 million
articles.summary: US News: A huge unfinished mansion in West Linn, Oregon, once owned by Hollywood Video founder Mark Wattles, is back on the market for $4.7 million, nearly thr.
articles.body: A huge unfinished mansion in West Linn, Oregon, once owned by Hollywood Video founder Mark Wattles, is back on the market for $4.7 million, nearly three decades after construction began. The 51,908-square-foot structure sits on a riverfront property and still lacks windows and finished floors. The property at 32020 S.W. Peach Cove Road has passed through three owners, but none has completed the mansion.The project began in 1994 when Wattles bought the 32-acre riverfront peninsula for $1.25 million, according to OregonLive. Wattles had started Hollywood Entertainment Corp. in Portland in 1988 and built it into a national chain with about 1,000 stores.Two years after buying the land, Wattles received a building permit. Construction began in 1997 on a structure planned to cover about 52,000 square feet. Wattles eventually put around $12 million into the project. The mansion was designed on a scale that made it comparable in size to the White House.The plan included nine bedrooms, 18 bathrooms, entertainment areas and a grand ballroom. There were also plans for showrooms for up to 60 collectible cars, garages, mechanic space and a 25-foot-high gym that could accommodate a full basketball court or an indoor swimming pool.A legal challenge changed courseThe project faced a legal challenge in 1997 from a neighbour who was supported by 1000 Friends of Oregon, a land-use advocacy group. The dispute centred on the large residential development being built on agricultural land.Wattles won the legal fight and retained the right to continue construction. However, the mansion was not completed. Wattles later moved to Las Vegas with his wife and five children, leaving the massive structure unfinished and wrapped to protect it from the weather.During construction, Wattles had also changed the design. The original plans called for a traditional style, but the design was later changed to a Northwest Craftsman style with a stone facade.The property eventually remained unfinished for years before Wattles decided to sell it. In 2018, it went to a live, no-reserve auction at The Nines Hotel in downtown Portland.New owner had a different visionRichard L Stanley, founder of Washington-based Rick's Custom Fencing & Decking, became the highest bidder at the 2018 auction. The sale closed for $2.27 million. At the time, Clackamas County had assessed the property at $5.3 million.Stanley had a different plan for the unfinished estate. He wanted to turn it into a Tuscan villa-style vineyard property with a wine-tasting room, according to the Lake Oswego Review.He invested about $1.5 million in a new roof and other improvements. He added piers that could support a future dock. Blueberries were also planted on the property as part of the requirements linked to Oregon's Exclusive Farm Use zoning.The agricultural zoning placed limits on residential development and required active commercial farming to maintain certain tax benefits. The blueberry planting was therefore part of the property's use under those rules.But Stanley's plans did not result in a completed mansion. In June 2020, only two years after buying the property, he put the unfinished structure on the market for $3.99 million. The listing was later removed without a sale.Mansion returns for $4.7 millionThe unfinished estate appeared again on regional listing services this year in May. This time, the asking price was $4.7 million.The property now covers about 29 acres and has water rights and around 2,700 feet of Willamette River frontage, including sandy beaches. Clackamas County currently assesses the property at about $4.1 million, while annual property taxes are listed at $46,947.Listing broker Jason Mendell of eXp Realty described the property as an opportunity for a buyer with a vision for an estate that would be difficult to recreate. Potential uses mentioned include a multigenerational family compound, a wellness destination and a legacy estate.Despite sitting unfinished for decades, the mansion already has much of its structural framework. The building includes steel beams, concrete and large glulam timber ceiling rafters. An elevator shaft also runs through the structure and could serve its different levels once construction is completed.Building permits have reportedly been kept active through seasonal maintenance. The structure has remained covered with synthetic protective material while waiting for the next stage of development.Property shaped by Oregon's land rulesThe property's location adds another unusual element to its history. A 2018 land-use analysis prepared for the auction said the mansion sits closer to the Willamette River shoreline than current setback rules would allow.That means the existing position of the structure cannot be legally recreated under today's local regulations, according to Platinum Luxury Auctions.Its agricultural zoning also continues to affect how the property can be used. Active agricultural production, such as the blueberry planting, is linked to the property's farm-use status and tax advantages.At the same time, the estate is close to the Oregon Golf Club and Aurora State Airport. It is also less than 30 minutes from downtown Portland and Portland International Airport.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Norway’s new king pays tribute to his late father as the country mourns
articles.summary: King Haakon VIII says King Harald represented Norway with ‘pride and joy’, promises to listen to Norwegians as monarch.
articles.body:
The new monarch of Norway, King Haakon VIII, has praised his late father, King Harald, for how he represented Norwegians, and promised to give everything for the country as king.

King Haakon gave his first speech as king on Saturday, which was aired live on television, a day after his father’s death.

“We are in mourning. At the same time, it brings us comfort and strength to know that so many are mourning with us,” he said, as reported by Norway’s public broadcaster NRK.

King Harald died on Friday at age 89 after 35 years as monarch. He suffered from haemolytic anaemia , which causes fatigue and shortness of breath.

“As king, my father represented Norway and the Norwegian people with pride and joy, through visits around the country, at events here at the royal palace, and while working on Norway’s behalf around the world,” Haakon said.

Tens of thousands of people gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo to pay their respects. Haakon thanked the public, saying it had been “a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, messages of condolence, and candles.”

The government has declared a national mourning period, which will last until after the funeral. A date has not yet been announced, but the Church of Norway will hold memorial services across the country on Sunday. In churches and city halls around Norway, people came to write in condolence books and light candles.

In his speech, Haakon said he and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit, and his daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would be present and listening.

“We believe in our popular government – and in democracy. We believe in a society built on law and justice – and where everyone is of equal value,” he said.

Haakon is due to take an oath to defend Norway’s constitution and laws before the legislature on Tuesday.

He becomes king in the wake of controversy surrounding his wife’s relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Haakon’s stepson, Marius Borg Hoiby , was also found guilty of rape, domestic violence other charges and sentenced to four years in prison in June.

articles.title: 8 officials suspended after probe into Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 newborns
articles.summary: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at an Islamabad hospital, his office said.
articles.body: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at an Islamabad hospital, his office said. Sharif issued the orders after an investigative committee headed by retired senior civil servant Shahid Khan presented its interim report on Wednesday’s fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, or PIMS, his office said in a statement. The fire was confined to a third-floor nursery but officials said it spread so quickly that staff were able to rescue only one baby from among the 15 being cared for there. The inquiry found that the nursery had no fire alarm or sprinkler system and that the hospital lacked detailed procedures and training for responding to fires and other emergencies, the statement said. The fire has intensified public anger, prompting grieving families and civil society groups to demand accountability. “Those guilty of criminal negligence deserve no leniency,” Sharif was quoted as saying. He ordered departmental and criminal proceedings against those identified by the committee. The eight included the hospital’s executive director, two joint executive directors, the head of the neonatal department, two other doctors, the hospital’s assistant director for security and the head of the Capital Development Authority’s emergency services. Sharif also approved action against a company responsible for hospital security and its officials. The government also already announced compensation of 5 million rupees (about $18,000) for each bereaved family. The statement said the interim inquiry found that supervisory staff were not on duty when the fire began. Two nurses, a female security guard and a house officer were in the ward. Emergency services were not called until six minutes after the fire started, and the first emergency responders arrived 15 minutes after receiving the call, the statement said. Investigators found that only two subsections of the hospital’s 13 standard operating procedures referred to fires or other emergencies. About two minutes of surveillance video of the nursery fire was shown during Saturday’s meeting. The footage was not immediately released. The interim report said a nurse risked her life to save a baby before the flames spread through the ward. Sharif approved a recommendation that she receive the Sitara-i-Khidmat, a state award recognizing public service. The deaths have prompted broader reviews of fire-safety measures at hospitals across Pakistan. The government in Punjab, the country’s most populous province, this week ordered an immediate review of fire-safety systems, firefighting equipment and emergency-response facilities at hospitals. Sharif earlier dismissed Health Secretary Aslam Ghauri, the Health Ministry’s highest-ranking civil servant, after the blaze. The fire was among Pakistan’s deadliest recent tragedies involving children. In June, 14 schoolchildren were killed when the roof of a tutoring center under construction collapsed in the eastern city of Lahore.
